title: Narada asks about the people
hookLine: Narada walks into the new hall and, instead of praising it, starts asking the king questions
carry: rajadharma: a leader's duty is the people's welfare

cards: A visitor walks into the new hall at Indraprastha and doesn't say a word about the building. Yudhishthira sits with his brothers, sages and kings around him.

Then Narada comes in, the wandering sage, with other rishis behind him. The Pandavas stand, bow, and give him a seat. And Narada, looking at the king who owns this wonder, begins to ask him questions.
Not about the crystal. About the kingdom.

teach.h: KACCIT: I HOPE THAT YOU ARE.
teach.b: Narada's questions run on and on, and in the Sanskrit they lean on a small word, kaccit. It asks while hoping the answer is yes, something like: I hope that you are. A few, in paraphrase.
Do you divide your time well between what's right, what's useful, and what's enjoyable? Are your ministers honest, and do they keep your counsel?
Do your soldiers get their pay and food on time? Do you look after the families of men who died serving you?
Do farmers have seed and food when they need it, and are there tanks and lakes, so farming doesn't hang on the rain alone? Notice where these go. The hall is right there, shining.
Narada's eyes go past it, to a soldier's widow, a farmer waiting for rain.

teach.h: RAJADHARMA: THE DUTY OF A KING.
teach.b: This has a name in Hindu teaching: rajadharma, the dharma of a king. The Mahabharata comes back to it again and again, and its answer is steady: the ruler is there for the people, not the people for the ruler.
A king in a crystal hall whose soldiers go unpaid has failed his dharma, however fine the hall. And the tone matters too. Kaccit doesn't accuse.
It says, I hope this is so, and leaves room for the king to answer, and to fix what isn't so yet. Yudhishthira bows and says he'll do what's been asked. The building is the occasion.

how: Narada's questions are read in Hindu tradition as a lesson in how to rule well, and they're often retold alongside the Mahabharata's other teachings on a king's duty, or rajadharma.

o: the crystal floor that fooled visiting kings
a hall where a king sits and hears his people
a sage's list of questions about ruling well

p: seed, food, and lakes, not rain alone

s: Narada praised the hall's crystal at length
he went straight past the building to questions about the kingdom.
Narada's questions asked about soldiers' pay
and about farmers, ministers, and the families of men who died in service.
Yudhishthira was offended by the questions
he bowed and said he would do what was asked.

games.q: you're Narada. the new king is sitting in the hall Maya built for him. what do you say?
o: ask how his soldiers, farmers and widows are doing.
warn him that pride comes before a fall.
games.why: he asks about the kingdom: ministers, soldiers' pay, farmers' seed, the families of the dead. the hall is the occasion; the people are the point.

practice: Choose one place where other people depend on you: a household, a team, a class, a friendship. Ask it one question the way Narada asks a king, beginning with I hope: I hope the people here are fed, I hope someone is being heard.
If you pray, hold those people before God as you ask; if you don't, just let the answer come, and notice what the question turns up.

wordCard.voice: Sabha. The hall where a king sits to hear his people. Today, Narada fills it with questions about rajadharma, each one asked in hope.

orig.note: Sanskrit kaccit: a word that opens a question hoping for yes, roughly 'I hope that…'. Narada's questions begin with it.

carryVoice: Your line: rajadharma: a leader's duty is the people's welfare. Narada asked about people, not crystal. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Lokapala Sabhakhyana Parva (Narada arrives and questions Yudhishthira on governance)
